newsitem.title: USA: US markets turn blind eye to Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: US markets turn blind eye to Deng's death.

text.p: U.S. financial markets took news of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping's death in stride on Wednesday, with the dollar popping briefly higher and stocks and bonds showing little reaction.
Market observers attributed the muted reaction to the fact that Deng's death was both widely anticipated and also unlikely to produce any immediate changes in Chinese policy.
Deng retired from politics in 1993, and Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin's formal assumption of the top leadership role has been carefully planned in anticipation of Deng's death.

"I don't think it has any implications for U.S. markets," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust in New York. "Even in the case of Pacific Rim markets, this news has been largely discounted over the last several years."
Rumours of Deng's ill health began circulating on Tuesday and inital reports of his death on Wednesday prompted a knee-jerk jump in the dollar.

The dollar rose to session highs of 1.7005 German marks and roughly 124.50 Japanese yen in the aftermath of the news, only to drift off those peaks by the time official word was released that Deng had died of complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection.

The dollar edged higher to close at 1.6980 marks against 1.6920 at the open and 1.6855 at Tuesday's close. The greenback also rose to end the day at 124.55 yen, up from 123.95 in early trade and 123.85 on Tuesday.

"Dollar-yen will be more affected due to the proximity and trade issues between the two nations, but any pressure on Asian currencies will be short-lived," predicted Doug Lee, a currency trader at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York.
The impact on the U.S. stock and bond markets was also subdued.

The Dow Jones industrial average stuck to narrow ranges after the announcement of Deng's death, although it later slid 47.33 points to end at 7,020.13 as investors took profits amid disappointment that the latest good news on U.S. inflation did not spark a rally.
U.S.-listed shares in China-related funds also showed little reaction to the Deng news. Chinese and Hong Kong American Depositary Receipts -- foreign shares traded in New York -- were also unmoved.
The 30-year Treasury bond was off 13/32, or $4.06 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.58 percent from 6.55 percent Tuesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Underscoring the muted reaction in the markets was news that ratings agency Moody's Investors Service would not change China's A3 sovereign debt rating in the aftermath of Deng's death.
Moody's said it had already accounted for Deng's eventual demise in its assessment of China's credit. The ratings agency saw no negative policy implications in Wednesday's news.

"Things are going fairly well for the Chinese," said Tom Byrne, a senior analyst at Moody's sovereign risk unit. "There are structural problems they have to deal with, but maybe now they'll start to deal with them with some uncertainty out of the way."
Standard and Poor's, the other major U.S. ratings agency, said on Tuesday that it would maintain a positive outlook on China's credit rating in the event of Deng's death.

Guido Cipriani, director of S&P's sovereign ratings group, said a de facto transfer of power to Communist Party chief Jiang would likely buffer any potentially destabilising side-effects of Deng's death in the near to medium term.
The subdued reactions in stocks and bonds were mirrored by a muted reaction in U.S. commodity markets, analysts said.

"China is a large player in several commodity markets, from copper to the grains, but Deng has been removed from power since 1993 and his death has been expected for some time," Refco New York commodity analyst James Steel said.
"China's demand for many basic commodities has been in a well-defined uptrend for some time and no discernible change is likely in the foreseeable future."
